title: Lean code at idle from cracked PCV hose
text: Applies to 2.0L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2012-2020. Some vehicles may set P0171 (system too lean, bank 1) with a rough idle that is worst on a cold engine. The PCV hose can crack on its underside where it joins the intake elbow, admitting unmetered air. With the engine idling, inspect the hose at the elbow and flex it gently while listening for a vacuum hiss. Repair: replace the PCV hose and clamp.
step: With the engine idling, inspect the PCV hose where it joins the intake elbow, flexing it gently while you listen for a vacuum hiss
results: I flexed the PCV hose at the elbow with it idling. No cracks and no hiss.
The PCV hose at the elbow looks fine, and I can't hear any hiss even when I bend it.

title: Lean code at idle from intake manifold gasket shrinkage
text: Applies to 2.0L I4 engines, model years 2021-2023, with the revised composite intake manifold. P0171 may set at idle after a cold soak because the manifold-to-head gasket shrinks at low temperature. Smoke-test the intake with the engine cold, concentrating on the manifold-to-head joint. Repair: replace the intake manifold gasket with the updated part.

title: Lean code at steady cruise from sticking purge valve
text: Applies to all gasoline engines with an EVAP purge valve. P0171 may set only during steady cruise above 50 mph on a fully warm engine; idle quality is normal and the code does not set at idle. With a scan tool, command the EVAP purge valve closed and check for vacuum at the canister side of the valve. Repair: replace the purge valve.

title: Extended crank on cold mornings from fuel pump check valve
text: Applies to 1.8L I4 and 2.0L I4 engines, model years 2010-2016. A long crank may occur only after the vehicle sits overnight below 40 deg F; restarts with a warm engine are normal. Leave a gauge on the rail test port overnight and compare the morning reading with the reading at shutdown. Repair: replace the fuel pump module.

title: Misfire in wet weather from coil boot tracking
text: Applies to all engines with coil-on-plug ignition. A misfire may occur at idle or light throttle only during rain or after a car wash, and it clears once the engine bay dries. Mist water over the coils with the engine idling and watch for arcing at the coil boots in a dark shop. Repair: install updated coil boots and apply dielectric grease.

title: Misfire at light load from intake valve deposits
text: Applies to 1.4L turbo I4 engines, model years 2016-2018. A misfire code may set at light-load cruise because carbon deposits on the intake valves disturb airflow on these direct-injection engines. Inspect the intake valves with a borescope through the intake port. Repair: clean the intake valves with the approved media-blast procedure.

title: High coolant temperature at sustained highway speed
text: Applies to all engines with a molded lower radiator hose. Coolant temperature may rise during sustained highway driving or towing while temperature in stop-and-go traffic stays normal. Inspect the lower radiator hose for collapse at high rpm with the engine warm. Repair: install the reinforced lower hose.

title: Temperature gauge reads high with normal coolant temperature
text: Applies to compact sedans with the 2.0L I4 engine, model years 2020-2022. The temperature gauge may read high in traffic while actual coolant temperature is normal. Compare the gauge with the coolant temperature reading on a scan tool. Repair: update the instrument cluster software.

title: Internal coolant loss at intake manifold gasket
text: Applies to 3.4L V6 engines, model years 2020-2022. Coolant loss with no external leak may come from the intake manifold gasket at a coolant passage. Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect the gasket area with a borescope through the throttle body opening. Repair: replace the intake manifold gaskets.

title: No heat from rear heater
text: Applies to minivans with a rear heater, model years 2010-2018. The front heater works normally but the rear vents blow cool because the rear heater control valve sticks closed. Command the rear heat on and feel both rear heater hoses under the vehicle. Repair: replace the rear heater control valve.

title: Dead battery after parking from audio module staying awake
text: Applies to midsize sedans and compact crossovers, model years 2021-2023. The battery may go flat after the vehicle is parked for two to three days because the audio module fails to enter sleep mode. After the vehicle has been locked for 60 minutes, measure draw at the negative battery terminal and note whether it drops below 50 mA when the radio fuse is pulled. Repair: reprogram the audio module.

title: Battery drain from infotainment head unit
text: Applies to full-size pickups with the 5.5L V8, model years 2021-2023. The infotainment head unit may not enter sleep mode after a software update and drain the battery within a few days. Measure parasitic draw and check whether the head unit stays awake. Repair: update the head unit software.

title: LED headlamp flicker from lamp driver software
text: Applies to midsize SUVs with LED headlamps, model years 2020-2022. Headlamps may flicker at idle while charging voltage is normal and no battery warning appears. Check the lamp driver module for stored codes. Repair: update the lamp driver module software.

title: Battery warning after auto start-stop restart
text: Applies to 1.4L turbo I4 engines with auto start-stop, model years 2019-2021. The battery warning lamp may flash briefly when the engine restarts after an auto stop. Review battery sensor data and stored body control codes. Repair: replace the battery monitoring sensor.

title: Slow crank after hot soak from starter heat
text: Applies to all vehicles. The engine may turn over slowly, but does turn over, when restarted after a hot soak. Measure starter current draw with an inductive clamp during cranking with fuel disabled. Repair: install a starter heat shield or replace the starter.

title: Intermittent no crank from starter relay in underhood fuse block
text: Applies to full-size pickups with the 5.5L V8, model years 2021-2023. The starter may intermittently fail to engage because of a weak starter relay in the underhood fuse block. Swap the starter relay with an identical relay and retest. Repair: replace the starter relay.

title: Low-speed pulsation felt in the seat from rear drums
text: Applies to hatchbacks with rear drum brakes, model years 2012-2015. A pulsation felt through the seat, not the steering wheel, may occur during light stops below 25 mph from out-of-round rear drums. Measure rear drum diameter at several points. Repair: replace the rear drums.

title: Brake vibration while towing
text: Applies to full-size pickups with the 5.5L V8, model years 2021-2023. A brake vibration may occur only during stops while towing a trailer over 5,000 lb. Check trailer brake gain settings and inspect rotors for heat spots. Repair: install revised front rotors.

title: Brake pull from caliper bracket casting
text: Applies to midsize SUVs, model years 2022-2024. A pull during braking may occur because of a front caliper bracket casting variation that holds the outer pad off-center. Inspect the bracket part number stamp against the bulletin list. Repair: replace both front caliper brackets.

title: Hard brake pedal at idle from booster check valve
text: Applies to 2.0L I4 engines, model years 2014-2017. The brake pedal may feel hard and require high effort at idle because the brake booster check valve sticks. Measure vacuum at the booster with the engine idling. Repair: replace the booster check valve and hose.

title: Rear clunk over bumps from leaf spring shackles
text: Applies to full-size pickups, model years 2013-2020. A clunk from the rear of the truck over bumps may come from dry leaf spring shackle bushings. Inspect the rear shackles for play with the truck on the ground. Repair: replace the shackle bushings.

title: Front clunk from loose subframe bolts
text: Applies to compact crossovers, model years 2021-2023. A clunk over bumps may come from front subframe mounting bolts that lost torque. Check subframe bolt torque. Repair: install new subframe bolts and torque to specification.

title: Steering wheel shake only when braking from highway speed
text: Applies to all vehicles. A steering wheel shake that occurs only when braking from highway speed, and is absent when cruising, usually comes from front rotor thickness variation. Measure rotor runout and thickness variation. Repair: replace or refinish the front rotors.

title: Warm air from passenger side only on dual-zone systems
text: Applies to all models with dual-zone automatic climate control. The driver side may blow cold while the passenger side blows warm because the passenger temperature door loses calibration. Run the climate control self-test and read stored HVAC codes. Repair: recalibrate the passenger temperature door actuator.

title: Warm AC after restart from electric compressor inverter
text: Applies to small crossovers with an electric AC compressor, model years 2022-2024. The AC may blow warm for several minutes after a restart because the compressor inverter is slow to initialize. Read compressor inverter codes with a scan tool. Repair: update the compressor inverter software.

title: Harsh 1-2 upshift on a cold transmission
text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2014-2020. A harsh 1-2 upshift may occur only during the first few minutes of driving below 40 deg F and stop once the transmission warms. Review the transmission fluid temperature reading during the event. Repair: update the transmission control software.

title: Harsh 2-3 upshift after a battery disconnect
text: Applies to full-size pickups with the 5.5L V8, model years 2021-2023. A harsh 2-3 upshift may occur after a battery disconnect because shift adaptive values were cleared. Run the shift adapt relearn drive cycle. Repair: reset the adaptive values and complete the relearn.

title: Lean codes at idle from a contaminated airflow sensor
text: Applies to gasoline engines with a mass airflow sensor. Some vehicles may set lean codes with high long-term fuel trim at idle because a contaminated sensor element under-reports airflow. With the engine at operating temperature and idling with all accessories off, read MAF airflow on a scan tool. Expect roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement (about 2-2.5 g/s for a 2.0L engine). Repair: clean the sensor element with an approved cleaner or replace the sensor.
step: With the engine warm and idling and the accessories off, read mass airflow on a scan tool and compare it with roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement
results: The scan tool shows the MAF right about where it should be for my engine size at idle.
MAF reading at warm idle matched the 1 g/s per liter rule almost exactly.

title: Long crank on hot restarts from fuel pressure bleed-down
text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. A long crank may occur on restarts after a short stop with a hot engine because rail pressure bleeds down and fuel boils in the hot rail. Drive until the engine is at full operating temperature, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and record the pressure 20 minutes later. Pressure should stay above 30 psi. Repair: replace the leaking injector or the fuel pump module.
step: Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the fuel rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later; it should still be above 30 psi
results: Put a gauge on after a drive. Still 42 psi after twenty minutes.
Residual pressure held at about 40 psi twenty minutes after shutdown.

title: Long crank on hot restarts from overfueling
text: Applies to all gasoline engines. Some vehicles may crank for several seconds before starting on a hot restart because the engine is overfueled. On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. If the engine starts noticeably faster in clear-flood mode, it is being overfueled on hot restarts. Repair: correct the overfueling source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.
step: On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator held to the floor to put the engine in clear-flood mode and note whether it fires noticeably faster
results: Tried it with the pedal floored on a hot restart. Cranked just as long, no difference.
The clear-flood trick made no difference. Still a long crank when it's hot.

title: Misfire under load from a tracked or fouled spark plug
text: Applies to all gasoline engines. A single-cylinder misfire under load or during acceleration may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the spark plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with a plug from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.
step: Pull the spark plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a good cylinder, checking the gap and looking for a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or fouling
results: Pulled the plug. Gap is 0.042, no cracks, and it looks like the others.
The plug from that cylinder looks clean and is gapped right, no tracking on the porcelain.

title: Overheating in traffic from an inoperative electric radiator fan
text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4, 2.5L I4, 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 1.4L turbo I4, 3.5L V6 and 3.4L V6 engines with electric radiator fans (not the 5.5L V8). Coolant temperature may climb at idle and in slow traffic while it stays normal at highway speed if the radiator fan does not run. With the engine at operating temperature and idling, turn the AC on or command the radiator fan on with a scan tool. The fan should start within a few moments. Repair: repair the fan circuit or replace the fan motor.
step: With the engine warm and idling, turn the AC on or command the radiator fan on with a scan tool and confirm the fan starts
results: Turned the AC on and the radiator fan kicked on right away.
Commanded the fan with my scanner and it spun up on both speeds.

title: Overheating at idle from a restricted radiator core
text: Applies to all engines. Temperature may climb at idle and in traffic when scale or debris restricts flow through the radiator core. With the engine at operating temperature and the thermostat open, use an infrared thermometer to compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical; a much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow. Repair: replace the radiator and flush the cooling system.
step: With the engine at operating temperature, compare the radiator inlet and outlet tank temperatures with an infrared thermometer and scan the core for cold spots
results: Inlet was 205 and outlet 172, and I didn't find any cold spots on the core.
About a 30 degree drop across the radiator and an even temperature across the core.

title: Coolant loss with no visible leak from an early-venting cap
text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans, small crossovers and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2021. The coolant level may drop slowly with no visible leak or puddle because the pressure cap vents early and coolant escapes through the overflow as vapor. Fit the radiator or reservoir cap to a cap adapter on the pressure tester and pump until the cap vents. It should hold at least its stamped rating. Repair: replace the pressure cap.
step: Test the radiator or reservoir cap on a cap adapter and confirm it holds at least its stamped pressure rating
results: The cap held its rated 16 psi on the adapter.
Tested the cap and it didn't vent until past its rating.

title: Weak heat in cold weather from a thermostat stuck open
text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4 and 2.4L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. Heater output may be weak in cold weather, with a temperature gauge that stays low, because the thermostat sticks partly open. From a cold start, idle the engine and watch coolant temperature on a scan tool while feeling the upper radiator hose. The hose should stay cool until about 195 deg F and warm quickly after that. Repair: replace the thermostat and gasket.
step: From a cold start, watch coolant temperature on a scan tool while feeling the upper radiator hose; it should stay cool until about 195 deg F
results: The upper hose stayed cool until the scanner showed about 196, and it got hot fast after that.
Reached 195 in about eight minutes and the upper hose warmed right at that point.

title: Cool vent air from a skipping blend door actuator
text: Applies to all models. Vent temperature may stay cool, with a clicking noise behind the dash, because the blend door actuator skips or stops short of full hot. With the engine warm, run the climate control from full cold to full hot while listening behind the center of the dash. The actuator should move smoothly through its full travel without clicking or stopping short. Repair: replace the blend door actuator and recalibrate it.
step: With the engine warm, sweep the temperature control from full cold to full hot and listen behind the center of the dash for the blend door actuator moving through its full travel
results: I can hear the door move all the way across and it doesn't click or stop.
The actuator sweeps smoothly from cold to hot, no clicking.

title: Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake
text: Applies to all vehicles. The battery may go flat after the vehicle is parked for several days because a control module or accessory circuit does not go to sleep. Close the doors, latch the hood switch closed and let the modules go to sleep, which can take up to 45 minutes. Connect an ammeter in series at the negative battery terminal without breaking the circuit. Draw should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate the circuit that stays awake by pulling fuses and correct the fault.
step: With the doors closed and the modules asleep, connect an ammeter in series at the negative battery terminal; draw should settle below 50 mA
results: Waited 45 minutes and the draw settled at 28 mA.
Meter read 0.03 amps once everything went to sleep.

title: Dim lights at idle from a slipping accessory belt
text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines with a belt-driven alternator, model years 2010-2020. Lights may dim at idle under electrical load because a glazed belt or weak tensioner lets the alternator pulley slip. With the engine off, inspect the accessory drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. Repair: replace the belt and tensioner.
step: With the engine off, inspect the accessory belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs and confirm the tensioner indicator is within its marked range
results: The belt looks new, no glazing, and the tensioner mark is in the middle of the range.
Belt and tensioner both look fine, no cracks.

title: Flickering lights from a failed alternator diode
text: Applies to all vehicles. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.
step: With the engine at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, measure AC ripple voltage across the battery posts and compare it with 0.5 V AC
results: Ripple was 0.08 volts AC.
AC ripple measured well under half a volt.

title: Click with no crank from the starter control circuit
text: Applies to vehicles with an automatic transmission or CVT. The starter may click or stay silent in park because the range switch, starter relay or wiring does not pass full voltage to the solenoid. Back-probe the starter solenoid S terminal and have a helper attempt a start in park. The S terminal should receive at least 10.5 V during the attempt. Repair: correct the range switch, relay or wiring fault that drops the voltage.
step: Back-probe the starter solenoid S terminal while a helper attempts a start in park; it should get at least 10.5 V
results: Got 11.8 volts at the S terminal when it clicks.
The S terminal sees about 11.5 V on the start attempt.

title: Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout
text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. A pedal or steering wheel pulsation may develop several thousand miles after a brake or wheel service when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the steering knuckle and set the plunger about 0.5 in from the outer edge of the rotor face. Rotate the rotor one full turn. Lateral runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it on the vehicle.
step: With the lug nuts torqued to spec, mount a dial indicator on the knuckle and measure front rotor lateral runout about half an inch in from the edge against the 0.002 in limit
results: Runout on both front rotors was 0.001 inch.
Dial indicator showed under a thousandth on both sides.

title: Pull during braking from binding caliper slide pins
text: Applies to vehicles with floating front calipers. The vehicle may pull to one side during braking because a corroded or swollen slide pin binds and causes uneven pad pressure. Remove each front caliper from its bracket without disconnecting the hose. Pull each slide pin from its bore and check for corrosion, swelling of the boot, or binding. Pins should move freely by hand through their full travel. Repair: clean and lubricate the pins, or fit new pins and boots.
step: Remove the front calipers from their brackets and confirm each slide pin moves freely through its full travel without binding
results: Slide pins on both sides slide freely, no rust.
Pulled the pins on both calipers. Clean and they move fine.

title: Brake pull from a restricted front brake hose
text: Applies to midsize sedans and compact crossovers, model years 2011-2020. A pull during braking, sometimes with one front wheel running hot, may come from a front brake hose that collapses internally and restricts fluid return. With the front wheels off the ground, have a helper press and release the brake pedal firmly. Immediately spin each front wheel by hand. Both wheels should turn freely right after release. Repair: replace both front brake hoses.
step: With the front wheels raised, have a helper press and release the brake pedal and spin each front wheel right away to see whether either one stays dragged
results: Both front wheels spin freely right after the pedal is released.
Neither wheel drags after letting off the pedal.

title: Front clunk over bumps from worn strut upper mounts
text: Applies to vehicles with front struts. A clunk or pop from the front over bumps or while turning at low speed may come from a worn strut upper mount or mount bearing. With a helper bouncing the front of the vehicle, rest a hand on the strut upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock. With the engine running, turn the steering lock to lock and feel for binding or a pop at the mount bearing. Repair: replace the strut upper mounts and bearings.
step: With a helper bouncing the front of the vehicle, rest a hand on each strut upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock
results: Couldn't feel any knock at the top mounts while it was bounced.
Strut mounts feel quiet and solid when bouncing the front.

title: Steering wheel shake at highway speed from wheel imbalance
text: Applies to all vehicles. A steering wheel shake that peaks in a narrow band such as 60-70 mph may come from wheel and tire assemblies that are out of balance or have high road-force variation. Check each wheel and tire assembly on a road-force balancer. Static and dynamic imbalance should be under 0.25 oz, and road-force variation should be under about 20 lb for passenger tires. Repair: rebalance the assemblies and match-mount any tire with high road force.
step: Check each wheel and tire on a road-force balancer for imbalance and road-force variation
results: A shop road-force balanced all four and they were all within spec.
Balance was fine on every wheel and the road-force numbers were low.

title: Pedal that sinks at a stop from master cylinder bypass
text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans and hatchbacks, model years 2010-2020. The brake pedal may slowly sink toward the floor while held at a stop, with no external leak, because fluid bypasses the master cylinder seals. With the engine off, pump the brake pedal several times to use up booster reserve. Apply steady, moderate pressure to the pedal and hold it for one minute. Repair: replace the master cylinder and bleed the system.
step: With the engine off and the booster reserve pumped out, hold steady moderate pressure on the pedal for one minute and watch whether it slowly sinks
results: Held it for a full minute with the engine off and the pedal didn't sink.
Pedal stayed put under steady pressure for the whole minute.

title: Warm AC at idle from an inoperative condenser fan
text: Applies to models with an electric condenser fan. Vent air may warm up at idle and in traffic and cool again at speed when the condenser fan does not run. With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises. Repair: correct the fan circuit fault or replace the fan motor.
step: With the engine idling and the AC on, confirm the condenser fan is running
results: The condenser fan comes on as soon as the AC is on.
Fan runs the whole time the AC is on.

title: Harsh engagement from high line pressure
text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission (not CVT or manual). Harsh engagements and firm shifts may occur when the pressure control solenoid holds line pressure high. Connect a pressure gauge to the line pressure test port. With the engine idling in drive and the brake applied, line pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. Repair: replace the pressure control solenoid.
step: Connect a gauge to the line pressure port and read line pressure at idle in drive with the brake applied; it should be 55-75 psi
results: Line pressure was 62 at idle in drive and rose normally.
Gauge read about 65 psi at idle in gear.
